title: Leaders Who Add Too Much Value
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay addresses passionate, knowledgeable leaders who unintentionally dominate meetings by contributing too many ideas, options, and suggestions. It argues this over-contribution discourages less experienced colleagues from speaking up and needlessly complicates decisions, even though the leader's intent is purely constructive. Because the pattern springs from confidence and a need for control rather than malice, the piece recommends coaching tactics — letting others speak first, contributing via questions instead of assertions — and reframes the leader's core job as elevating everyone else's ideas rather than showcasing their own.
points: Identifies a paradox where well-intentioned, high-value contributions from a passionate leader can still crowd out the team's own thinking.
Notes over-contributing leaders are often genuinely unaware of the chilling effect their input has on quieter colleagues.
Recommends concrete coaching fixes: let others speak first, and shift from making assertions to asking questions.
Traces the root cause to a combination of self-confidence and a need to control outcomes, not malice or ego alone.
Reframes leadership's core job as elevating others' ideas and growth rather than maximizing the leader's own visible contribution.
quotes: But in their enthusiasm to influence others with their insights, leaders can sometimes go too far. They can add too much value and throw a wrench into the discussion that isn’t always obvious to them.

By being quick to offer too many ideas, suggestions, and options, they undermine the contributions of others, discourage those with less experience from sharing their ideas, and make decision-making much more complex than it needs to be.
Coaching these leaders and team members to allow others to speak first can help them understand the negative impact they normally have on discussions.
The urge to contribute their ideas and suggestions in every discussion, even when it’s unnecessary, usually springs from a combination of self-confidence and the need to control outcomes.
Convincing those with this affliction that a leader’s job is to highlight everyone else’s ideas so they can grow and develop can start a personal transformation.
